power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

**`setwd()` in the code**

**7 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. text.text: Leadership emergence in socially egalitarian contexts depends on the qualities of individuals and on how others perceive their capacity to use them.
Multi-Capital Leadership theory proposes that leaders deploy material, social, somatic, and neural capital to solve problems of group living by providing benefits to group members or imposing costs.
Conflict resolution is one important leadership domain.
We reanalyse peer rankings of 60 adults in a relatively egalitarian community of Chabu foragerhorticulturalists in southwest Ethiopia.
Seven peer-raters ranked participants on twelve traits identified as relevant to leadership in contemporary evolutionary theories.
A previous analysis averaged rankings before modelling, obscuring differences among raters and treating positions within an ordering as continuous measurements.
Here, we fitted a multivariate Plackett-Luce model directly to the individual rankings.
This accounts for dependence within rankings and incorporates uncertainty into estimates.
It also allows us to estimate consensus orderings and systematic variation associated with rater sex.
Male and female peer-raters produced broadly similar orderings, including for conflict resolution.
This could reflect actual covariation in participants' qualities, a shared evaluative schema, or both.
Peer-ranked proxies for material, social, and neural capital covaried closely and did not form clearly separable perceptual domains.

The clearest descriptive contrast was between benefit-related attributes, including conflict resolution, sound decision-making, and prosociality, and cost-related attributes, including being feared and fighting.
Conflict-resolution reputation was most closely associated with decision-making, kin support, respect, and intelligence, and showed no clear positive association with fighting.

In these rankings, a reputation for conflict resolution was more clearly distinguished from aggression and coercion than were measures capturing the three capital domains represented in the instrument.

Conflict resolution is a common function of leaders across human societies, though who intervenes and how they intervene varies (Diekmann, 1985; Garfield & Glowacki, 2023; Garfield, Syme, & Hagen, 2020; Smith et al., 2016).

text.text: Among mobile foragers, disputants can often move away from one another, and residential flexibility can limit the escalation of conflict (Kelly, 2013; Woodburn, 1979).
text.formatted: Among mobile foragers, disputants can often move away from one another, and residential flexibility can limit the escalation of conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Kelly, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Woodburn, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: High mobility, however, does not completely obviate the need for third-party mediators because conflicts among neighbours, economic partners, friends, and family still threaten group cohesion (Garfield, 2021; Lee, 2018; Woodburn, 1979).
text.formatted: High mobility, however, does not completely obviate the need for third-party mediators because conflicts among neighbours, economic partners, friends, and family still threaten group cohesion <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Garfield, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lee, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Woodburn, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Ethnographic research has documented mediation, coalition-based punishment, and other norm-enforcement systems among relatively egalitarian populations.
The form these systems take appears to vary with socioecology (Garfield et al., 2026 (Garfield et al., , 2023;; Molho, De Petrillo, Garfield, & Slewe, 2024; Singh & Garfield, 2022; Wiessner, 2020).

text.text: In the absence of prescribed or institutionalised conflict mediation roles, individuals capable of resolving conflicts are likely to have unique capacities.

Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists, for example, who resolves conflicts has been linked to body size, kinship, alliance strength, and gender (Glowacki & von Rueden, 2015; von Rueden, 2023; von Rueden, Alami, Kaplan, & Gurven, 2018).

text.text: Evolutionary accounts of leadership often contrast dominance with prestige, and physical formidability with knowledge and culturally valued skills (Chapais, 2015; Cheng, 2019; Cheng, Tracy, Foulsham, Kingstone, & Henrich, 2013; Durkee & Lukaszewski, 2024; Henrich & Gil-White, 2001; von Rueden, 2014).

text.text: Multi-Capital Leadership (MCL) integrates this empirical and theoretical work (Garfield, von Rueden, & Hagen, 2025; von Rueden, 2014).
text.formatted: Multi-Capital Leadership (MCL) integrates this empirical and theoretical work <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Garfield, von Rueden, & Hagen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">von Rueden, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: It proposes that leaders draw on their material, social, somatic, and neural capital to solve recurrent problems of group living by providing benefits to group members, which can include valuable advice, or imposing costs (Durkee, Lukaszewski, & Buss, 2020; Garfield et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It proposes that leaders draw on their material, social, somatic, and neural capital to solve recurrent problems of group living by providing benefits to group members, which can include valuable advice, or imposing costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Durkee, Lukaszewski, & Buss, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Garfield et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Dominance and prestige can emerge from different underlying forms of capital in different contexts.

Conflict resolution is one domain in which leadership capital can be deployed, along with providing counsel, coordinating cooperation, punishing transgressors, and distributing resources (Garfield et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Conflict resolution is one domain in which leadership capital can be deployed, along with providing counsel, coordinating cooperation, punishing transgressors, and distributing resources <ref type="bibr">(Garfield et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Smith et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In this framework, capital (the resources and traits a leader has) can be distinguished from function (how a leader uses them, such as providing benefits or imposing costs).
The ability to mediate a dispute is therefore not itself a form of capital, but a perceived capacity to deploy capital in ways that have social consequences and often provide benefits.

In a previous analysis of peer-ranked data collected among a Chabu community, Garfield & Hagen (2020) found that nearly all leadership traits covaried strongly and positively, with a median correlation of 𝑟 = 0.58 among all measures except fighting.
text.formatted: In a previous analysis of peer-ranked data collected among a Chabu community, <ref type="bibr">Garfield & Hagen (2020)</ref> found that nearly all leadership traits covaried strongly and positively, with a median correlation of 𝑟 = 0.58 among all measures except fighting.

text.text: The traits stemmed from several accounts of leadership, including dominance-prestige, sexual and social selection, and embodied-capital models (Cheng et al., 2013; Garfield, Hubbard, & Hagen, 2019; Henrich & Gil-White, 2001; Kaplan, Mueller, Gangestad, & Lancaster, 2003; Neel, 1980).
text.formatted: The traits stemmed from several accounts of leadership, including dominance-prestige, sexual and social selection, and embodied-capital models <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cheng et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Garfield, Hubbard, & Hagen, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Henrich & Gil-White, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kaplan, Mueller, Gangestad, & Lancaster, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Neel, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: This covariation prevented clear adjudication between competing theoretical models.
The covariation could reflect true dependencies among various qualities.

Health or intelligence, for example, could be causally linked to several domains, such as good decision-making skills or interpersonal skills (Kaplan et al., 2003; von Rueden, Gurven, Kaplan, & Stieglitz, 2014).
text.formatted: Health or intelligence, for example, could be causally linked to several domains, such as good decision-making skills or interpersonal skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kaplan et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">von Rueden, Gurven, Kaplan, & Stieglitz, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: High social status could also influence judgements of particular qualities through a shared evaluative schema, such as a halo effect (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977).
text.formatted: High social status could also influence judgements of particular qualities through a shared evaluative schema, such as a halo effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Nisbett & Wilson, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: The two processes are not mutually exclusive.
This earlier analysis averaged the rankings for each trait for each participant before modelling in a measurement error model, obscuring differences among peer-raters.
Retaining each ranking retains useful data but requires a specialised analysis.
By modelling the raw rankings of individual raters, we incorporate uncertainty within and between raters and can also examine systematic differences associated with rater sex.
Agreement between the sexes could reflect participants' actual qualities, a shared evaluative schema, or both.

The current study, which reanalyses previously published data (Garfield & Hagen, 2020 , 2026), examines peer perceptions of twelve leadership-relevant attributes among Chabu forager-horticulturalists in southwest Ethiopia, with conflict resolution as a focal domain in which local leaders emerge.
text.formatted: The current study, which reanalyses previously published data <ref type="bibr">(Garfield & Hagen, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2026)</ref>, examines peer perceptions of twelve leadership-relevant attributes among Chabu forager-horticulturalists in southwest Ethiopia, with conflict resolution as a focal domain in which local leaders emerge.

text.text: The study community has a history of egalitarianism and, at the time of data collection, was undergoing socio-political change.
Influence remained partly ephemeral and domain-specific, as is common in egalitarian societies, even as leadership was becoming more formalised through institutionalised roles.
We pursue three exploratory aims.
First, we estimate consensus rankings and assess how closely male and female peer-raters agree.

Second, we examine whether associations between traits, which were chosen to test the dominance-prestige, sexual selection, and embodied-capital models of leadership, before MCL theory was formulated, correspond to the proxies for the three represented forms of capital or to benefit-related and cost-related capacities.
Third, we identify the qualities peers associate with a reputation for resolving conflicts.
Rather than modelling rankings averaged across peer-raters, we fit a Plackett-Luce model directly to individual rankings, an analytic technique uncommon in human behavioural ecology.
The Chabu are forager-horticulturalists who live in the Sheka forests of southwest Ethiopia.
Until the late 1990s, many were mobile hunter-gatherers subsisting on hunted game, wild yams, and collected honey (Dira & Hewlett, 2016 , 2017).
text.formatted: Until the late 1990s, many were mobile hunter-gatherers subsisting on hunted game, wild yams, and collected honey <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dira & Hewlett, 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: At the time of data collection (summer 2016), subsistence at the study site combined hunting (via spear-hunting with dogs or snare traps), foraging of wild tubers, greens, and beans, with most calories from maize and yam horticulture.
Community members also produced cash crops and goods, including coffee, honey, and pottery, on a limited scale (unpublished field notesfoot_0 ).
text.formatted: Community members also produced cash crops and goods, including coffee, honey, and pottery, on a limited scale (unpublished field notes<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> ).

text.text: Chabu political relations have historically been relatively egalitarian, with social influence emerging contextually within particular activities rather than through institutionalised roles (Garfield & Hagen, 2020; Taye, 2015).
text.formatted: Chabu political relations have historically been relatively egalitarian, with social influence emerging contextually within particular activities rather than through institutionalised roles <ref type="bibr">(Garfield & Hagen, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Taye, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Leadership tended to be associated with collective hunting, construction, and the resolution of inter-individual conflicts or community problems (Dira & Hewlett, 2017; Garfield & Hagen, 2020).
text.formatted: Leadership tended to be associated with collective hunting, construction, and the resolution of inter-individual conflicts or community problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dira & Hewlett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Garfield & Hagen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Since the early 2000s, Chabu communities have also participated in Ethiopia's kebele administrative system.
The kebele is the smallest administrative unit of the Ethiopian state, similar to a form of neighbourhood organisation.
Under this system, communities elect leaders responsible for security, schools, churches, and justice, with authority to impose fines and incarceration.
Selection for these roles were conducted via a public show-of-hands vote and continued to reflect Chabu values concerning respect, prosociality, and community service (Garfield & Hagen, 2020).
text.formatted: Selection for these roles were conducted via a public show-of-hands vote and continued to reflect Chabu values concerning respect, prosociality, and community service <ref type="bibr">(Garfield & Hagen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: At the time of fieldwork, the study community combined what we term a relatively egalitarian social structure with a recently introduced system of democratically elected local leadership.
The term allows for inequalities across domains and subgroups.
Egalitarian and hierarchical processes can coexist within the same community and operate differently across contexts (Stibbard-Hawkes & von Rueden, 2025; von Rueden, 2023).
text.formatted: Egalitarian and hierarchical processes can coexist within the same community and operate differently across contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Stibbard-Hawkes & von Rueden, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">von Rueden, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In relatively egalitarian settings, such as among the Chabu, leadership is often achieved rather than ascribed and remains contingent on others' willingness to defer (Boehm, 1999).

text.text: Peer rankings provide quantitative evidence that allows us to examine the structure and agreement of these evaluations.
Approval for the research and data collection was obtained from the Washington State University Institutional Review Board (IRB no.
14445), Hawassa University College of Social Sciences and Humanities, the Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples' Regional State Office of the President, and community elders and leaders.
Participants consented to the collection and use of their portrait photographs in the peer-ranking procedure.
We reanalyse the Chabu peer-ranking data introduced by Garfield & Hagen (2020) and subsequently updated (Garfield & Hagen, 2026).

text.text: The data include rankings of 60 adults (34 men and 26 women) from a convenience sample in a community of approximately 250 people.
Interviews were conducted privately in the Chabu language.
Those present were the participant, a local research assistant, an external research assistant, and ZHG.
Interviews took place at participants' homes, at their field shelters, or at the researcher's accommodation in the community.
Participants consented to having a portrait photograph taken for the peer-ranking procedure.
Each photograph showed the participant's head and shoulders against a neutral background.
Seven community members (four men and three women) were recruited as peer-raters based on their ability to work effectively with the research team.
For each prompt, a peer-rater viewed an array of photographs of either male or female participants on a digital screen.
The peer-rater selected the person who best fit the prompt; that photograph was removed, and the peer-rater then selected the next person.
This continued until the remaining photographs had been ordered.
Male and female participants were ranked separately.
Self-rankings and rankings of spouses were excluded.
The present analysis is restricted to twelve traits for which the original prompts are documented and rankings are available for both male and female participants (Table 1).

We assigned the twelve traits to categories informed by Multi-Capital Leadership theory 175 before interpreting the associations among them.

Seven traits serve as peer-ranked 176 proxies for capital types: farming for material capital; allies, kin, respect, and likable for 177 social capital; and intelligent and expertise for neural capital.
Five traits are closer to perceived capacities or behavioural reputations: conflict, decisions, and prosocial are treated as benefit-related, whereas feared and fighting are treated as cost-related.
These assignments follow the definitions in Garfield et al. (2025) and are theoretical rather than estimated from the data.

text.text: These assignments are approximate.
Each measure is a peer perception, not a direct measure of capital or behaviour.
No ranked trait measures somatic capital.
Farming is the sole proxy for material capital and may also reflect physical capacity and skill.
Respect and likable may partly result from earlier influence.
Likewise, feared measures others' response to perceived cost-imposing capacity, whereas fighting measures a behavioural reputation.
Benefit generation and cost imposition are not mutually exclusive in MCL theory: conflict resolution, for example, can benefit a group while imposing costs on particular disputants.
We therefore use the categories as an exploratory framework for comparing patterns of association, not as a confirmatory measurement model or a classification of mutually exclusive leadership types.
The peer-ranking procedure produced an ordering for each combination of trait, peer-rater, and participant sex.
Earlier analyses converted these orderings to relative ranks, rank/rank !"

text.text: That conversion is convenient but loses and distorts information in three ways.
It treats the gap between adjacent ranks as equal throughout, when an ordering carries no information about spacing.
It treats each peer-rater-by-participant value as an independent observation, when the values within a ranking are a permutation and so are strongly dependent.
It also offers no way to express that a participant placed in the middle of a ranking is located far less precisely than one placed at either end.
We fit a multivariate Plackett-Luce (mvPL) model directly to the rankings.
Each participant has a latent score on each trait, and the scores covary across traits.
The model includes participant age as a covariate and systematic score differences associated with rater sex.
Fitting the original orderings carries ranking uncertainty into estimates of trait associations, age gradients, and rater-sex differences.

The benefit-related traits are most closely associated with the proxies for social and neural capital and intercorrelate with one another between 0.57 and 0.72.

The two cost-related traits are most closely associated with the proxy for material capital, are weakly or negatively associated with the proxies for social and neural capital, and correlate 0.45 with each other.
Associations across the two sets are weaker: conflict resolution correlates 0.23 [-0.01, 0.45] with feared and -0.12 [-0.35, 0.11] with fighting.
The proxies assigned to material, social, and neural capital are generally positively correlated.
There is little evidence that they form separate perceptual domains.

Proxies for social and neural capital are about as closely associated with one another (mean 0.62) as the social proxies are among themselves (0.59), and the two neural proxies, intelligent and expertise, correlate 0.53, less closely than intelligent correlates with likable (0.73 [0.55, 0.86]) or respect.

The pattern is consistent with a descriptive distinction between benefit-related and costrelated reputations, but the grouping and imprecise partial correlations do not support a claim that peers classify the traits into discrete MCL categories.

The broad positive covariation reported in the earlier analysis (Garfield & Hagen, 2020) is also evident in our improved modelling of the original peer rankings that directly preserves the ordering produced by each peer-rater and carries uncertainty in those orderings into the estimated associations among traits.

text.text: Male and female peer-raters produced similar orderings for most traits, including conflict resolution.
At the same time, the three capital domains represented in the instrument do not appear as clearly differentiated perceptual domains.
The clearest descriptive contrast is between benefit-related and cost-related traits.
Within that pattern, conflict-resolution reputation is associated with sound decision-making, kin support, respect, and intelligence.
There is no clear association with fighting.
Similar orderings among male and female peer-raters show that the estimated structure is shared across the two rater-sex groups.
Such agreement is expected both when rankings reflect participants' actual qualities and when they reflect an evaluative schema shared by the raters.
The present model also does not estimate persistent departures by individual peer-raters.
The distinction between actual qualities and perception remains unresolved.
These findings therefore concern the structure of shared peer perception.
Conflict resolution occupies a distinct position within that shared perception.
Peer-raters associate it most strongly with making sound decisions and with kin support, respect, and intelligence.
There is little evidence of a positive association with a reputation for fighting, and the association with being feared is weak.
Mediation behaviour and conflict outcomes were not observed, so these results cannot establish which qualities actually make a mediator effective.
The rankings also leave open whether highly ranked individuals intervened frequently or exercised influence through selective restraint.
Such restraint is documented in other relatively egalitarian contexts.
Among the Ju/'hoansi, respected camp figures were expected to mediate rather than punish, and often declined to join punitive coalitions (Wiessner, 2005, pp. 131, 138).

text.text: Within these Chabu rankings, a reasonable conclusion is that a reputation for resolving conflict is connected more closely to cognitive and social evaluations than to a reputation for interpersonal aggression.
This distinction is consistent with ethnographic accounts of Chabu leadership and their cultural model of leaders.
Good kebele leaders are described as people who solve community problems, do not fight or spread rumours, and respond to disagreement without becoming easily angered (Garfield & Hagen, 2020).
text.formatted: Good kebele leaders are described as people who solve community problems, do not fight or spread rumours, and respond to disagreement without becoming easily angered <ref type="bibr">(Garfield & Hagen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A leader who repeatedly displays aggression may be advised by elders and eventually replaced.
Kebele offices themselves carry powers of sanction, including fines and incarceration.
In this context, the capacity to impose costs is now vested largely in social roles rather than in personal aggression.
This may help explain why a reputation for resolving conflicts was not associated with a reputation for fighting.

The associations with kin support, respect, intelligence, and sound decision-making also suggest that conflict resolution in this community may rely on prosocial strategies that draw on detailed knowledge of community relationships.
Kebele positions are unpaid.
Officeholders typically describe their duties as a burden and would prefer to focus on their own work (Garfield & Hagen, 2020).
text.formatted: Officeholders typically describe their duties as a burden and would prefer to focus on their own work <ref type="bibr">(Garfield & Hagen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Leaders in relatively egalitarian settings often bear costs and receive little in return for their service (Seabright, 2022; von Rueden et al., 2014).

text.text: Among the Chabu, this relatively new formal authority exists alongside culturally endogenous norms constraining personal aggression.

These dynamics fit a process-based account of egalitarianism, in which social checks on dominance can operate alongside formal inequalities in influence and power (Stibbard-Hawkes & von Rueden, 2025; von Rueden, 2023).

text.text: We did not test this interpretation directly.
Future research on conflict mediation and sanctioning could do so.
The results are consistent with some aspects of MCL theory.
Peers appear to distinguish benefit-related from cost-related functions, but they do not clearly distinguish the forms of capital that MCL proposes underlie them.
The benefit-related traits intercorrelate and are most closely associated with the proxies for social and neural capital.
The two cost-related traits, feared and fighting, are associated with one another and have similarly ordered associations with the remaining traits.
The strength and direction of these associations differ: all ten posterior median associations of feared with the remaining traits are positive, compared with only one for fighting.

This contrast is consistent with arguments that conventional measures of dominance may conflate distinct affordances, including the ability and willingness to impose costs (Durkee & Lukaszewski, 2024; Durkee et al., 2020).

text.text: The present measures do not distinguish those affordances directly.
These patterns suggest that peers distinguish, at least descriptively, between a reputation for providing benefits and a reputation for imposing costs.
The same individuals may nevertheless do both.
These patterns do not establish two discrete types of leaders.
Distinctions among the represented forms of capital are less apparent.
Proxies for material, social, and neural capital covary positively, and the partial correlations are too imprecise to identify unique associations.

The proxies for social and neural capital are about as closely associated with each other as the social capital proxies are with one another, and intelligent is more closely associated with respect and likable than with expertise, the other proxy for neural capital.
This pattern has at least three possible explanations.
Individuals high on one form of capital may also tend to be high on others, so that the forms are distinct but strongly correlated in this community.
Alternatively, peer perceptions of each form may reflect a more general evaluation, such as overall standing or competence, that the prompts do not separate.
These possibilities remain unresolved in the present data.
The exploratory clustering suggests a third possibility (Figure S3).

text.text: The identified communities combine particular elements from different MCL categories: intelligent with respect and likable, allies with decisions and conflict, and expertise with kin and prosocial.
The partition is weak and should not be overinterpreted.
The clustering suggests, however, that broad capital categories may obscure how specific components of social and neural capital relate to one another and to particular leadership functions.
The available prompts may not measure each category equally.
Testing MCL will require measuring components of each form of capital separately.
The instrument was developed in 2016 from dominance-prestige, sexual selection, and embodied-capital models, before MCL theory was formulated (Garfield & Hagen, 2020; Garfield et al., 2025).

text.text: These measures were not designed to test MCL.
The association between farming and feared illustrates the problem.
Horticultural productivity can reflect land and material output, but it also depends on sustained physical labour and skill.
In this setting, the sole proxy for material capital may therefore incorporate somatic and neural capital.
More direct and independent measures of all four forms of capital will be needed for a proper theoretical test.
These data also stem from a community undergoing political change.
By 2016, the Chabu had participated in the kebele system for approximately a decade.

Formal roles assigned different functions to particular people, while older norms of egalitarianism continued to associate influence with broad competence and prosocial community service (Dira & Hewlett, 2017; Garfield & Hagen, 2020).

text.text: The strong covariance among many traits may reflect that broader evaluative pattern.
These cross-sectional data leave open whether formal roles were producing more specialised reputations or whether peer perception was changing over time.
The participant sample is small and was recruited by convenience from one interconnected community.
Only seven people served as peer-raters, and they were selected partly because they worked effectively with researchers.
Coverage also varies across traits and peer-raters.
Modelling the original orderings avoids treating ranks as independent continuous measurements and accommodates incomplete rankings.
Selection effects or bias in the rankings could still have influenced results.
The rater-sex component is estimated from only two or three peer-raters of each sex for any given participant-sex and trait combination.
Individual idiosyncrasies are therefore confounded with rater sex, and the model contains no individual-rater latent effects.
Agreement between the estimated male-and female-rater orderings suggests broadly shared perception across these two small groups.
Evidence that all community members would agree remains limited.
All twelve traits are peer rankings.
We do not observe conflict mediation, its effectiveness, the type or severity of conflicts, or the capital that participants actually deploy in particular disputes.
We also lack complete kinship and social-network data with which to examine relationships between peer-raters and ranked participants.
A shared evaluative schema is therefore a reasonable interpretation, alongside real covariation among the underlying qualities.
Distinguishing them will require independent behavioural, demographic, or physiological measures alongside a larger number of peer-raters.
The model estimates 66 free correlations from 34 male and 26 female participants.
The partial correlations are consequently imprecise, and none has a 90% credible interval excluding zero.
Our claims therefore concern zero-order associations.
Unique effects remain unresolved.
The primary model also estimates a correlation matrix shared across male and female participants.
Rankings were produced separately for the two participant sexes, so the latent scores indicate positions within each sex.
Differences in level between men and women cannot be inferred from these scores.
Finally, the MCL comparison covers only three of the four forms of capital.
Somatic capital has no peer-ranked indicator, and material capital is represented only by farming.
The assignments are theoretical, were applied retrospectively, and include traits that may represent both resources and outcomes of prior social interaction.
The function-capital comparison therefore offers an exploratory organisation of the observed associations.
It has not been validated as a measurement model.
Directly modelling the Chabu peer rankings shows that male and female peer-raters share broadly similar perceptions of leadership-relevant qualities.
Within those perceptions, a reputation for resolving conflicts accompanies sound decision-making, kin support, respect, and intelligence.
There is no clear association with a reputation for fighting.
The three represented forms of capital are less clearly differentiated: their peer-ranked proxies covary and do not form distinct perceptual domains in these data.
This pattern is consistent with the MCL distinction between capital and the functions for which it is deployed.
It also shows the difficulty of measuring theoretically distinct forms of capital through peer rankings alone.
The findings concern shared perceptions.
Individual qualities and mediation effectiveness were not independently observed.
Within this relatively egalitarian Chabu community, conflict-resolution reputation is associated with perceptions of neural and social capital.
